title: Why Do You Suddenly See New Things Everywhere?
summary: The frequency illusion, or Baader–Meinhof phenomenon, is a cognitive bias where you notice a concept more often after recently becoming aware of it.
evidenceNote: The core phenomenon is well-documented, with consensus pointing to interactions between selective attention and confirmation bias.

scenes.text: Ever learn a new word and suddenly hear it everywhere?
This is known as the frequency illusion, or the Baader–Meinhof phenomenon.
It happens due to two psychological processes: selective attention and confirmation bias.

items.title: Selective Attention
items.detail: Filtering for what you are currently focusing on.

items.title: Confirmation Bias
items.detail: Seeking evidence that confirms your beliefs while overlooking the rest.

scenes.text: After mentioning a German militant group once in 1994, Terry Mullen kept noticing the name in the news.
In reality, the frequency of the object has not changed; your brain is just filtering for it.
Your brain simply notices what it is currently looking for.
emphasis: notices what it is currently looking for
